settings.title: Fistula
settings.body: A surgically joined vein and artery in your arm, and the most common long-term access. It needs to stay reachable during the whole session — and kept warm and protected in between.
settings.tip: Clothing: a sleeve that opens fully to the upper arm, so it never has to be rolled or removed.

settings.title: Graft
settings.body: A soft tube placed under the skin to connect a vein and artery, used when a fistula isn't suitable. Cared for much like a fistula, with the same warmth and access needs.
settings.tip: Clothing: wide, non-compressive sleeves — nothing tight over the graft site.

settings.title: Catheter
settings.body: A line in the neck or chest, often used while a fistula matures. Needs to stay clean and dry, with the dressing kept covered.
settings.tip: Clothing: a front-open top so the team can reach the line without anything going over your head.

settings.title: Weigh-in and settling
settings.body: You're weighed to measure fluid gained since last time, then settled into your chair. Bring a warm layer — centres run cold by design.

settings.title: Connection
settings.body: A nurse connects your access to the machine. With a fistula this means two needles; with a catheter, the line is attached. A sleeve that opens fully makes this quick and private.

settings.title: The run
settings.body: Your blood is filtered and returned, continuously. Your access arm stays still — most people read, watch something, nap, or work one-handed. Warmth and comfort matter most here.

settings.title: Disconnection
settings.body: The machine returns the last of your blood, needles come out, and pressure is held on the site until bleeding stops. You're weighed again before you leave.

settings.title: Recovery
settings.body: Some people feel tired or washed-out afterwards, others feel fine. Plan a gentle rest of day for your first few sessions until you know how your body responds.

settings.title: A sleeve-access top or hoodie
settings.body: Opens fully for fistula or graft access — warm, but never in the way.

settings.title: A lap-size warm blanket
settings.body: Not king-size — large blankets catch on tubing.

settings.title: Headphones & a tablet on a stand
settings.body: Your access arm stays still, so one-handed entertainment wins.

settings.title: Warm socks & a neck pillow
settings.body: Feet get cold even under a blanket; an arm-support pillow eases strain.

settings.title: Approved snacks & a water bottle
settings.body: Check with your dietitian about fluid and what's right for you.

settings.title: A small bag for it all
settings.body: Pack it the night before so a session day never starts in a rush.

settings.title: Work & routine
settings.body: Many people keep working. If you have an evening class or shift, ask about a day-time slot — schedule dialysis around your life, not your life around dialysis.

settings.title: Travel
settings.body: Dialysis centres exist in most cities and countries. With a few weeks' notice, your unit can help arrange sessions away from home so you can still take the trip.

settings.title: Diet & fluid
settings.body: Your dietitian will guide you on fluid, potassium, phosphate, and salt. It feels like a lot at first — within a few weeks it becomes second nature.

settings.title: Staying warm
settings.body: Cold sensitivity is real — centres are air-conditioned and dialysis lowers your core temperature. Layers you can add and remove one-handed make every session easier.

settings.title: Your emotions
settings.body: It's normal to feel a wave of grief, anger, or fear early on. Talk to your team, lean on others on the same path, and be patient with yourself.

settings.title: Feeling like you
settings.body: You are not a patient in a gown — you're you, going to an appointment. Clothing that looks and feels like your own changes how the whole day feels.

settings.question: Will dialysis hurt?
settings.answer: Connecting a fistula involves two needles, which can sting at first — most people find it becomes very manageable, and numbing cream is available. A catheter connection isn't painful. The run itself shouldn't hurt; tell your nurse if anything feels wrong.

settings.question: How should I dress for a session?
settings.answer: Wear something warm with easy access to your arm (for a fistula or graft) or chest (for a catheter). Sleeve-zip tops, button or snap fronts, and soft layers you can add and remove with one hand are ideal. Avoid anything tight over the access site.

settings.question: Can I still travel?
settings.answer: Yes. With planning, your unit can arrange "holiday dialysis" at a centre near your destination. Give a few weeks' notice and carry a summary of your treatment details with you.

settings.question: Will I be able to keep working?
settings.answer: Many people do. Talk to your unit about scheduling sessions around your hours — early-morning, evening, or weekend slots are often available, and home dialysis offers even more flexibility.

settings.question: Why am I so cold during treatment?
settings.answer: Centres are kept cool for infection control, and dialysis itself lowers your core temperature. Anaemia, common in kidney disease, can add to it. A warm layer that still allows access is the single most-recommended comfort item.
